Next, suppose we do not know the matrix F. Then kσ ∗ k1 = 1. This can be shown by proving the contrapositive. Assuming the negation 1 < kσ ∗ k1 := a, there exists a vector x ∈ [−1, 1]p such that x> σ ∗ = kσ ∗k1 > 1. If each of the columns of F is equal to x, then by definition of the slack ∗ function, −γ σa > −γ(σ ∗ ), so σ ∗ cannot be optimal. In other words, if we want to protect ourselves against the worst case F, then we have to set kσk1 = 1 so as to ensure that C(σ) is empty. In this case, the slack function simplifies to γ(σ) = −b> σ, over the probability simplex. Minimizing this is achieved by setting σi to be 1 at arg max bi i∈[p] and zero elsewhere. So as might be expected, in the case that F is unknown, the optimal strategy is simply to use the classifier with the best error guarantee. This is true because C(σ ∗ ) is empty, and the set of all σ such that C(σ ∗ ) is empty is of wider interest. We dub it the Zero Box Region: ZBR = {σ : C(σ) = ∅}. Another clean characterization of the ZBR can be made by using a duality argument similar to that used to prove Theorem 2.
